label: The Jones Polynomial
notes: Open the lecture. The Jones polynomial revolutionized knot theory and earned a Fields Medal. The lecture builds it from the Kauffman bracket by correcting for writhe, records its defining skein relation, computes examples, and highlights both its power and its still mysterious geometric meaning for oriented knots and links.

label: From Bracket to Jones
notes: Repair the bracket by multiplying by minus A cubed raised to the negative writhe, producing the normalized bracket that is invariant under all three Reidemeister moves. Substituting A to the minus four for the variable t turns this into the Jones polynomial, a genuine ambient isotopy invariant of oriented knots and links.

label: The Jones Skein Relation
notes: Present the oriented skein relation satisfied by the Jones polynomial, linking the positive crossing, the negative crossing, and the oriented smoothing through a linear equation in t and its square root. Together with the value one on the unknot this relation alone determines the invariant recursively, paralleling the Conway construction.

label: Computing Examples
notes: Compute the Jones polynomial of the trefoil and the Hopf link from the skein relation. The two trefoils of opposite handedness give mirror-image polynomials, so Jones detects chirality where the Conway polynomial cannot. This sensitivity to mirror images is one of the invariant's most celebrated and immediately useful features.

label: Power and Mystery
notes: Discuss what Jones can and cannot do. It distinguishes vast numbers of knots and detects chirality, yet it is unknown whether it detects the unknot, and its deeper meaning emerged only later through statistical mechanics, operator algebras, and quantum field theory. Its discovery opened the entire field of quantum invariants.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. The Jones polynomial is the writhe-corrected Kauffman bracket, an ambient isotopy invariant obeying its own oriented skein relation. It detects chirality and separates many knots, while its geometric meaning links to physics. The next lecture turns to braids and the algebra underlying these invariants.
